```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>",
  message = FALSE,
  warning = FALSE
)
library(dataRetrieval)
library(duckdb)
library(dplyr)
```

A new data warehouse contains continuous and daily time series data as cloud-native Parquet files indexed via the USGS' Water Data SpatioTemporal Asset Catalog (STAC) API. This new pathway makes it fast and easy to discover and download large amounts of water data.

The most authoritative, up-to-date version of a record can be retrieved from the OGC API services. OGC data are retrieved in the original "read_waterdata" functions. However, if you need lots of data, the new STAC functions are for you!

The files on the STAC system do not necessarily have the latest available data. They get updated frequently, but there's no promise of when the files get refreshed. If needed, you can fill in more recent data using OGC data. 


There are two main pathways to take advantage of this new STAC service:

1. **Classic workflow**: functions that return all requested data into your R environment. Because it's so easy to request a LOT of data, care is needed to prevent running out of memory.

2. **Flexible workflow**: functions that give users search, download, and open STAC data.

Before you start exploring the new functions, we recommend requesting a **NEW** USGS API token from here: <https://api.waterdata.usgs.gov/signup/>, and saving it as "STAC_USGS_PAT" in your .Renviorn (perhaps using `usethis::edit_r_environ()`).

```
STAC_USGS_PAT = "my_new_token"
```
The request limits for STAC are much higher than OGC. However, the STAC requests will drain your OGC limits quickly. This is why having separate tokens for each service is recommended.


# Classic Workflow

The new functions are `read_waterdata_continous_por` and `read_waterdata_daily_por`. The "por" stands for period of record. These functions are especially efficient when you want data spanning the full period of record. These functions are for users who want to pull a "reasonable" amount of data into their R environment. 


## read_waterdata_continuous_por

Possibly the best use-case for these new STAC function is for a user who wants the full period of record continuous data for a single site. Using the original OGC functions, this required looping many requests since the OGC continuous service limits requests to a 3 year period. In one test, it took 35 minutes to download all the data for a site that had nearly 30 years of continuous sensor data of 8 parameter codes. Using the STAC function, it took ~6 seconds. Here we wrap the call with `system.time` to show how long it took to retrieve the data:

```{r continous, eval=FALSE}
library(dataRetrieval)

system.time({
  df <- read_waterdata_continuous_por(
    monitoring_location_id = "USGS-0208458892"
)
})
#> user  system elapsed 
#> 4.21    0.69    6.74 

nrow(df)
#> [1] 3104851
```

Over 3 million rows in seconds - not too bad!

There are more arguments that give you additional flexibility to query your data. Keep in mind that there's A LOT of continuous data, and it becomes really easy to request more data than R can load into memory. 

We built into the function two arguments that will limit your ability to accidentally ask for a ridiculous amount of data. `site_limits` and `memory_MB_limit`.

The `site_limits` argument is set as a default of 100 sites for the continuous data. If the STAC search determines that there will be more than the `site_limits`, it will not even attempt to 

The `memory_MB_limit` argument set it as a default as 1000 (so, approximately 1 GB of data returned). If you request more than that, the function will error. You can bump up the `memory_MB_limit` if you are confident in your computer's memory. 

Here is an example of a request that will fail because the number of sites exceeds the `site_limit` default:

```{r showError, eval=FALSE}
dane_data <- read_waterdata_continuous_por(
    state_name = "Wisconsin"
)
```

```
Error in get_stac_data(args, data_type = data_type, collections = collection,  : 
  Unique monitoring_location_id exceed site_limits
```

This is fewer sites, but still a LOT of data. This example should fail due to exceeding the `memory_MB_limit`: 

```{r showAnotherError, eval=FALSE}
wisconsin_data <- read_waterdata_continuous_por(
    state_name = "Wisconsin",
    county_name = "Dane County",
    parameter_code = "00060",
    site_type = "Stream",
    site_limits = 300
)

```

```
Estimated memory size of the dataset:5925.91 MB

Error in check_memory(data_tbl$total_rows, memory_MB_limit, ncol = ncol(df_out)) : 
  Increase the memory_MB_limit parameter to allow this query to be loaded.
```

## read_waterdata_daily_por

Similar to the continuous data, we can now retrieve period of record daily data quicker using the `read_waterdata_daily_por` function. As an example, we could request all the daily data for a single HUC. 

```{r hucDaily, eval=FALSE}
df_huc <- read_waterdata_daily_por(
    hydrologic_unit_code = "07090002",
    parameter_code = "00060"
)
nrow(df_huc)
```

```
472717
```

## Further Considerations

Each time you run one of the "por" functions, the code will go to the STAC service, find the files you need, access and load the data into memory. Under the hood, it's using (duckDB)[https://duckdb.org/docs/2.0/clients/r/overview].

If you are asking for large amounts of data, consider using the flexible workflow shown below.

If you need to fill in more recent data, consider querying the OGC data on "last_modified".

```{r OGCfill, eval=FALSE}
df <- read_waterdata_continuous_por(
  monitoring_location_id = "USGS-01435000",
  parameter_code = "00060")

latest_modified <- max(df$last_modified)
latest_modified
#> [1] "2026-11-24 05:26:19 UTC"

df_new <- read_waterdata_continuous(
  monitoring_location_id = "USGS-01435000",
  parameter_code = "00060",
  # get everything modified after "latest_modified"
  # here we do that by adding a second:
  last_modified = c(latest_modified + 1, NA) 
)

range(df_new$time)
#> [1] "2026-11-24 05:30:00 UTC" "2026-11-25 18:15:00 UTC"

df_all <- df |> 
  dplyr::bind_rows(df_new)

range(df_all$time)
#> [1] "1987-04-01 05:15:00 UTC" "2026-11-25 18:15:00 UTC"
```

# Flexible Workflow

What if you are asking for TONS of data? There are 3 main functions that allow you to search, (optionally) download, and then lazy load the data. What does it mean "lazy load the data"? A connection is established to the data files (either pointed at a local download or the files in the cloud) using duckDB. We will show a few examples of how the data can be explored with this connection without needing to load the entire dataset into memory. 

## Search -> Open Lazy Tibble

The function `search_stac` let's us search the STAC. Available arguments are similar to those found in `read_waterdata_monitoring_location`. In this example, we're querying for all the daily STAC data available for Dane County, Wisconsin:

```{r search1}
features_county <- search_stac(
    county_name = "Dane County",
    state_name = "Wisconsin",
    site_type = "Stream",
    collections = "daily"
)
```

The result of this function is a list with all the information that the next set of functions need to access the raw STAC files.

Next, we can use that list to create a connection to the data in the cloud with the `open_stac` function. First, we need to create a connection. The function `initial_connection` establishes the connection and adds your `STAC_USGS_PAT` token to the request headers. It is important to remember to close your connection when you are done using `DBI::dbDisconnect`.

```{r openCon, eval=FALSE}
con_1 <- initial_connection()

data_tbl <- open_stac(features = features_county,
                      con = con_1)

```

`data_tbl` is now a "lazy tibble". This mean you can use it as an input of any `dplyr` type commands. The full query is not sent until you `dplyr::collect()` the data. Before you run `dplyr::collect`, you can get some interesting information from the lazy tibble, all without loading the full dataset into memory:

```{r lazytibble, eval=FALSE}
data_tbl
```

If we want to perform that entire summary and load the summary into memory:

```{r nonlazy, eval=FALSE}
data_summary <- data_tbl |> 
  dplyr::summarise(
    min_date = min(time, na.rm = TRUE),
    mean_val = mean(as.numeric(value), na.rm = TRUE),
    count = dplyr::n(),
    .by = c(monitoring_location_id, parameter_code) 
  ) |> 
  dplyr::collect()
```

If you needed a subset of the data:

```{r getsub, eval=FALSE}
df_subset <- data_tbl |> 
  dplyr::filter(
    monitoring_location_id %in% c("USGS-05427945",
                                  "USGS-05406483")
  ) |> 
  dplyr::collect()

```

Or, if you were confident that your computer could load all the data into R:

```{r loadall, eval=FALSE}
df <- data_tbl |> dplyr::collect()

```

There are many cool things to explore with a lazy tibble. Once you are done with your analysis, close the connection:

```{r close, eval=FALSE}
DBI::dbDisconnect(con_1)
```

## Search -> Download

The workflow above hit the data in the cloud - and every time you explored the data, some-to-many requests are generated. There are a variety of reasons you would prefer to have your data local. You can use the function `download_stac` to copy all of the STAC files from the `search_stac` function. The files are downloaded in a HIVE partitioned set of parquet files. The partitioning is done by monitoring_location_id. 

Let's download all the continuous data that is available in the New York City area:

```{r nyc_download, eval=FALSE}
features_nyc <- search_stac(
    county_name = c("New York County",
                    "Kings County",
                    "Queens County",
                    "Bronx County",
                    "Richmond County"),
    state_name = "New York",
    collections = "continuous"
)

dir.create("nyc", showWarnings = FALSE)

download_path <- download_stac(
  features = features_nyc,
  file_directory = "nyc", 
  output_returned = "partition_folder"
)

download_path
#> "nyc/continuous"
```

Inside the download folder, there is one subfolder per collection ("continuous" in this case). Within that, each monitoring location gets its own `monitoring_location_id=<id>` folder holding that site's parquet file(s). This is the Hive partitioning layout, where the folder names carry the partition key and value:

```
nyc/
└── continuous/
    ├── monitoring_location_id=USGS-01302020/
    │   └── historical.parquet
    ├── monitoring_location_id=USGS-01372043/
    │   ├── historical.parquet
    │   └── current.parquet
    ├── monitoring_location_id=USGS-01376307/
    │   └── historical.parquet
    └── ...
```

If you download more than one collection (for example `collections = c("daily", "continuous")`), each collection gets its own sibling folder:

```
nyc/
├── continuous/
│   ├── monitoring_location_id=USGS-01302020/
│   │   └── historical.parquet
│   └── ...
└── daily/
    ├── monitoring_location_id=USGS-01302020/
    │   └── data.parquet
    └── ...
```

Because the partition key is encoded in the folder names, duckDB (and Arrow) can skip folders that don't match a filter on `monitoring_location_id`, so only the relevant files are read.

Now that the 

### Lazy Tibble

The `open_stac` function works the same way on local files as it does on the cloud files shown earlier. Instead of the list returned by `search_stac`, pass it the path returned by `download_stac`. Nothing is loaded into memory until you call `dplyr::collect()`.

```{r openLocal, eval=FALSE}
con_nyc <- initial_connection()

nyc_tbl <- open_stac(
  features = download_path,
  con = con_nyc
)

nyc_tbl
```

Use `dplyr` verbs to filter and summarize. The query runs in duckDB against the local parquet files:

```{r openLocalQuery, eval=FALSE}
nyc_summary <- nyc_tbl |>
  dplyr::filter(
    monitoring_location_id == "USGS-01302020",
    parameter_code == "00060"
  ) |>
  dplyr::mutate(value = as.numeric(value)) |>
  dplyr::summarise(
    min_val = min(value, na.rm = TRUE),
    mean_val = mean(value, na.rm = TRUE),
    max_val = max(value, na.rm = TRUE),
    count = dplyr::n()
  ) |>
  dplyr::collect()
```

To bring a subset into R as a data frame:

```{r openLocalCollect, eval=FALSE}
df_site <- nyc_tbl |>
  dplyr::filter(
    monitoring_location_id == "USGS-01302020",
    parameter_code == "00060"
  ) |>
  dplyr::collect()
```

Close the connection when you are done:

```{r closeLocal, eval=FALSE}
DBI::dbDisconnect(con_nyc)
```

### duckDB SQL

If you prefer SQL to `dplyr`, you can send raw SQL strings to duckDB with `DBI::dbGetQuery` (returns a data frame) and `DBI::dbExecute` (runs a statement and returns the number of affected rows). DuckDB's `read_parquet` function reads the downloaded files directly, and the `**` wildcard matches every partition folder.

```{r sqlCon, eval=FALSE}
con_sql <- initial_connection()

# Count the rows in the downloaded files:
DBI::dbGetQuery(
  con_sql,
  "SELECT COUNT(*) AS n_rows
   FROM read_parquet('nyc/continuous/**/*.parquet')"
)
```

A summary by site and parameter code, computed in duckDB. Only the summary table is loaded into R:

```{r sqlSummary, eval=FALSE}
sql_summary <- DBI::dbGetQuery(
  con_sql,
  "SELECT
     monitoring_location_id,
     parameter_code,
     MIN(time) AS start_time,
     MAX(time) AS end_time,
     COUNT(*) AS n_obs,
     AVG(TRY_CAST(value AS DOUBLE)) AS mean_val
   FROM read_parquet('nyc/continuous/**/*.parquet')
   GROUP BY monitoring_location_id, parameter_code
   ORDER BY monitoring_location_id, parameter_code"
)
```

`value` is stored as text, so `TRY_CAST(value AS DOUBLE)` converts it and returns `NULL` for anything that can't be converted. To pass values into a query safely, use `?` placeholders and the `params` argument rather than pasting strings together:

```{r sqlParams, eval=FALSE}
df_site <- DBI::dbGetQuery(
  con_sql,
  "SELECT *
   FROM read_parquet('nyc/continuous/**/*.parquet')
   WHERE monitoring_location_id = ?
     AND parameter_code = ?",
  params = list("USGS-01302020", "00060")
)
```

If you run several queries against the same files, create a view once and query it by name. `dbExecute` runs statements that don't return rows:

```{r sqlView, eval=FALSE}
DBI::dbExecute(
  con_sql,
  "CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW nyc_continuous AS
   SELECT * FROM read_parquet('nyc/continuous/**/*.parquet')"
)

DBI::dbGetQuery(
  con_sql,
  "SELECT parameter_code, COUNT(*) AS n_obs
   FROM nyc_continuous
   GROUP BY parameter_code
   ORDER BY n_obs DESC"
)
```

Close the connection when you are done:

```{r sqlClose, eval=FALSE}
DBI::dbDisconnect(con_sql)
```

### Arrow

The [arrow](https://arrow.apache.org/docs/r/) package can also open the partitioned folder. `arrow::open_dataset` reads the `monitoring_location_id=` folder names and adds `monitoring_location_id` as a column. Nothing is loaded into memory until you call `dplyr::collect()`. 


```{r arrow, eval=FALSE}
library(arrow)
library(dplyr)

# Point to the collection folder inside the download directory:
nyc_ds <- open_dataset(
  "nyc/continuous",
  format = "parquet",
  partitioning = hive_partition(monitoring_location_id = large_utf8())
)

nyc_ds
```

```
FileSystemDataset with 187 Parquet files
11 columns
time_series_id: large_string
monitoring_location_id: large_string
parameter_code: large_string
statistic_id: large_string
time: timestamp[us, tz=UTC]
value: large_string
unit_of_measure: large_string
approval_status: large_string
qualifier: list<element: string>
last_modified: timestamp[us, tz=UTC]
method_category: large_string
```

The parquet files already store `monitoring_location_id` as a `large_string`. By default, arrow reads the same value from the folder name as a regular `string`, and the two types can't be merged. That produces the error `Field monitoring_location_id has incompatible types: large_string vs string`. Declaring the partition field as `large_utf8()` makes the two types match.

Use `dplyr` verbs on the dataset to filter and summarize. The filter on `monitoring_location_id` is applied to the folder names, so only the matching files are read:

```{r arrowQuery, eval=FALSE}
nyc_summary <- nyc_ds |>
  filter(
    monitoring_location_id == "USGS-01302020",
    parameter_code == "00060"
  ) |>
  mutate(value = as.numeric(value)) |>
  summarise(
    min_val = min(value, na.rm = TRUE),
    mean_val = mean(value, na.rm = TRUE),
    max_val = max(value, na.rm = TRUE),
    count = n()
  ) |>
  collect()
```

To bring a subset into R as a data frame:

```{r arrowCollect, eval=FALSE}
df_site <- nyc_ds |>
  filter(
    monitoring_location_id == "USGS-01302020",
    parameter_code == "00060"
  ) |>
  collect()
```

## Further Considerations

### Updating "Hot" Continuous Data

### Re-partition Examples

The sweet spot of hive partitioning is 100MB-1GB per individual parquet file. Too big or too little of files cause different kinds of bottlenecks. The individual monitoring_location_id files that come from the STAC service are almost universially smaller than this. Here is an example of how to take the monitoring_location_id partitioning, and re-partition it to state_name:

```{r repartition, eval=FALSE}
library(duckdb)
library(dplyr)
library(dataRetrieval)

con_1 <- initial_connection()

sites <- read_waterdata_combined_meta(
  state_name = c("Alaska", "Wisconsin"),
  parameter_code = "00060",
  statistic_id = "00003",
  skipGeometry = TRUE
)

site_features <- search_stac(
  monitoring_location_id = unique(sites$monitoring_location_id),
  collections = "daily"
)

dir.create("pqts", showWarnings = FALSE)

# Default is partitioned folder:
dwnlwd <- download_stac(
  site_features,
  file_directory = here::here("pqts"),
  overwrite = FALSE
)

con_1 <- initial_connection() 

# By default, duckdb will go up to 80% of system RAM
# If you want to change that, you can do it like this:
# dbExecute(con_1, "SET memory_limit = '1GB';")
# My regular laptop has 32GB installed RAM

register_data <- open_stac(features = dwnlwd, 
                      con = con_1) |> 
  filter(time_series_id %in% sites$combined_meta_id) |> 
  left_join(sites |> 
              select(monitoring_location_id, state_name),
            by = "monitoring_location_id",
#copy = "inline" is OK if sites df is smallish, 
# if it's bigger use copy = "temp-table":
            copy = "inline") |>   
  duckdb::duckdb_register(conn = con_1, name = "state_partitions")

dir.create("state_discharge", showWarnings = FALSE)

DBI::dbExecute(con_1, dplyr::sql("COPY (
    SELECT *
    FROM state_partitions
  ) TO 'state_discharge' (FORMAT PARQUET, PARTITION_BY (state_name))
")) 

duckdb::duckdb_unregister(con_1, "state_partitions")
DBI::dbDisconnect(con_1, shutdown = TRUE)

```

### Target Workflow

You can use these functions in a targets workflow. Here is an example of a _targets.R file that could be used. In this example, we first find all the daily mean discharge in Alaska. In the `download_stac` function, we can set the argument `output_returned = "targets"`, then the result of that function will be a vector for the full path for all of the downloaded files. This vector can then be used in a dynamic branch in the next step:

```{r target, eval=FALSE}
library(targets)
library(tarchetypes)

tar_option_set(
  packages = c(
    "tidyverse",
    "dataRetrieval",
    "here"
  )
)

dir.create("pqts", showWarnings = FALSE)

list(
  tar_target(
    name = sites,
    command = read_waterdata_combined_meta(
      state_name = "Alaska",
      parameter_code = "00060",
      statistic_id = "00003",
      skipGeometry = TRUE
    )
  ),
  tar_target(
    name = site_features,
    command = search_stac(
      monitoring_location_id = unique(sites$monitoring_location_id),
      collections = "daily"
    )
  ),
  tar_target(
    name = dwnlwd,
    command = download_stac(
      site_features,
      file_directory = here("pqts"),
      output_returned = "targets"
    )
  ),
  tar_target(
    cleaned_data,
    clean_files(x = dwnlwd, sites = sites),
    pattern = map(dwnlwd),
    iteration = "vector"
  )
)
```
